facts.statement: The type species Eocypselus vincenti was named by C.J.O. Harrison in 1984 based on fossils from the London Clay Formation of England.
facts.quote: Fossils of E. vincenti, the Eocypselus type species (comprising a wing and pectoral bone) were initially recognized from the London Clay Formation of England and named by C.J.O. Harrison in 1984.

facts.statement: The species Eocypselus rowei was described in 2013 by Ksepka and colleagues.
facts.quote: A second Eocypselus species, E. rowei was described in 2013 by Ksepka and colleagues.

facts.statement: Researchers named the species E. rowei in honor of John Rowe, whom they considered a "fossil geek."
facts.quote: The discoverers chose to honor Rowe, whom they considered to be a "fossil geek."

facts.statement: Mayr and Kitchener described three additional Eocypselus species in 2024.
facts.quote: In 2024, Mayr and Kitchener described three additional species.

facts.statement: Ksepka stated that Eocypselus represents the closest known relative to the point where swifts and hummingbirds diverged.
facts.quote: Eocypselus shares features in common with both hummingbirds and swifts, leading Ksepka to declare that it "represents the closest we've gotten to the point where swifts and hummingbirds went their separate ways".

facts.statement: The species E. rowei was less than 5 inches from head to tail.
facts.quote: E. rowei was less than 5 in from head to tail.

facts.statement: In E. rowei, feathers made up more than half of the wingspan.
facts.quote: Its feathers made up more than half the size of its wingspan.

facts.statement: Eocypselus is a basal form of the order Apodiformes, which includes hummingbirds, tree swifts, and swifts.
facts.quote: Eocypselus is a basal form of the order Apodiformes, which traditionally includes hummingbirds, tree swifts, and swifts.

facts.statement: Eocypselus lived during the Ypresian stage, between 56 and 48.07 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Ypresian to Ypresian (56 to 48.07 million years ago)
